accuracy.evidence: Checked for the insect body plan: three tagmata (head, thorax, abdomen), six jointed legs all on the thorax, one pair of antennae and the compound eyes on the head, wings (when present, one or two pairs) on the thorax with the flight muscles inside it, chitin exoskeleton shed by moulting (ecdysis) as the insect grows and most adults no longer moulting, against the Natural History Museum and Royal Entomological Society insect anatomy pages and the DfE NC Y3/Y4 science programme. The comparison animals were checked too: spiders are arachnids with 8 legs and 2 body parts (cephalothorax and abdomen), woodlice are isopod crustaceans with 14 legs, centipedes have one pair of legs per segment (far more than 6), worker ants are wingless insects, and butterflies have 4 wings (two pairs). Parameterised answers 6*n, 3*n, 8*n and 4*n give whole numbers at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented primary misconceptions about invertebrates (Allen, Misconceptions in Primary Science; ASE/Nuffield guidance on classification): legs on the abdomen because it is the biggest part (prediction option, red warning legs and a miss message in the leg step, challenge tag abd, mastery m8), every minibeast or bug being an insect (spider, woodlouse and centipede cards with their own messages, challenge tags mini and spider, mastery m2), a wingless ant not counting as an insect (sort-step message, mastery m4), and insects having bones that grow or a case that stretches (prediction option, the eat-twice message 'A hard case cannot stretch', challenge tags bones and stretch, mastery m3).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaginsect is built on this topic's own structure: an ant-shaped body whose three ellipse segments are hit targets for naming, a leg box whose legs only attach to the thorax (wrong segments flash red with a reason), antenna, eye and wing cards that must land on the head or thorax and then appear on the drawing, an eat-then-moult cycle where a tight exoskeleton blocks growth until the old case is shed, and a sorter whose cards are drawn with their real segment and leg counts. It is not a relabelled sorter like flagmbhab (habitats) or the minibeast move lab, and the gate reports under 30% shingle overlap with every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner meets each rule by doing it before the text states it: legs refused by the head and abdomen show where they join; the antennae, eyes and wings appear on the drawing only on the right segment; eating while the case is tight is refused and only a moult lets the insect grow, which shows why an exoskeleton must be shed; and the sort step reveals the count of legs and parts after a wrong answer, so counting becomes the test. Each step's summary comes only after the task is done.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 2 or 6 body parts (the naming step finds exactly three), legs on the abdomen or on every part (the leg box refuses both), the skeleton inside like ours or no hard parts (the case blocks growth until it is moulted), and a spider counting as an insect because it is a minibeast or has wings (the spider card is refused with its 8 legs and 2 parts shown). The task message echoes the locked-in choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five challenge questions with two wrong options each, every one mapped to its own message: abd (the abdomen is biggest but legs do not join it), headleg (the head carries eyes and antennae), spider (8 legs is a spider), size (big or tiny, still 6 legs and 3 parts), mini (minibeast just means no backbone), looks (a woodlouse looks like a beetle but has 14 legs), antthor, abd2, bones and stretch. In-lab mistakes also name the slip, e.g. 'That is the abdomen, the big back part. The thorax is the smaller middle part.'

readability.evidence: validate_lessons.py passes the learner limits: kid text reads at about FK grade 2 and adult text at about grade 5. Kid sentences are short and concrete ('Every insect has six legs. All six join the thorax.'), and the precise Year 3–4 words are used and explained: head, thorax, abdomen, antennae, exoskeleton, moulting, minibeast, insect.

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matches. Each lab step has one job (name the parts, place legs, place sense organs and wings, grow by moulting, classify) and every feedback line carries a count or a body part. Item explanations give the reason (6 legs and 3 parts, the case cannot stretch) instead of restating the question.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px in light and dark theme on every step, before and after Show me. First-pass fixes: the body drawing lost its antennae, eyes, wings and labels because the segment helper had no y value (fixed); the antenna card was hidden behind the feedback box and now sits under the heading; the Head and Thorax labels touched, so the Head label moved above the body. Buttons are full-size and wrap; the sort card shows the minibeast drawn large with its name.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button: 'Head (front part)', 'Thorax (middle part)', 'Abdomen (back part)', 'Leg on thorax' and the other two, 'On the head/thorax/abdomen' for each card, 'Eat and grow' and 'Moult', and 'Insect', 'Not an insect' and 'Count for me'. The canvas aria-label states the task and progress after each move ('3 of 6 legs attached to the thorax.'), and challenge feedback is an aria-live status. walk.cjs reports axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) clean in light and dark on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors; the canvas keeps a light card in dark mode.
